papers.title: An ODE to Changing Variables: $v = y/x$ Is For Victory
papers.abstract: Most first courses in differential equations introduce students to very special differential equations which can be solved in closed form from a small set of techniques (such as separable equations and integrating factors). Frequently other equations can be converted to one of these forms through a change of variable; however, these transformations are usually just given without any explanation of \emph{how} people found them, or \emph{why} problems of these forms have nice solutions, but not related ones. We consider the first order differential equation $dy/dx = f(x,y)$ where $f(x,y)$ does not factor as $A(x)B(y)$, and assume $f(x,y) = g(y/x^r)$ for some nice function $g$ and some real number $r$. This can be reduced to a separable equation only when $r=1$. We then discuss generalizations and what conditions on $f$ lead to a change of variables yielding a separable equation. Our goals are twofold. First, to encourage students and instructors to be active, questioning the methods and results, seeing how far they can be extended and why they work. Second, we discuss how to appropriately use AI to take ideas and special cases as prompts and quickly create extensions and editable notes that can be shared with students, freeing up professors (and students) from straightforward calculations \emph{without} sacrificing learning and understanding.

papers.title: From Objective Compromise to Structure-Enabled Intelligence: Reshaping the Scientific Paradigm of AI
papers.abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), are fundamentally constructed upon the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm. This paradigm can be characterized as an ill-posed optimization problem within a high-dimensional parameter space. When confronted with real-world scenarios characterized by noise and conflicting constraints, the logic of global error minimization inherently induces a strong smoothing effect. Consequently, this yields statistical compromise solutions that flatten local features, making it arduous to overcome the inherent bottleneck of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing AI models generate outputs purely based on statistical probabilities. They lack the capacity to autonomously discern truth from falsehood or establish causal logic, thereby lacking genuine cognitive intelligence. To address the ontological limitations of the OD paradigm, this paper proposes a novel paradigm termed \textit{Structure-Enabled Intelligence}. This approach abandons the conventional path of relying solely on computing power scaling and data fitting to achieve emergent intelligence. Instead, it embeds mathematical structures and physical mechanisms as underlying priors into the algorithmic architecture, constraining the model's solving process with structured scientific rules. Through this paradigm shift from ``data-driven objective fitting'' to ``mechanism-structure dominance,'' the proposed approach fundamentally mitigates the issue of statistical compromise, enhances the model's extrapolation and generalization capabilities, and simultaneously reshapes human-AI synergy by upholding human subjectivity in scientific cognition.

papers.title: Frege's logic in Grundgesetze is nonclassical
papers.abstract: I show that the axioms and rules of inference about the horizontal in the subsystem of Grundgesetze without value-ranges fail to capture its intended interpretation. That is, I build a nonstandard model in which $-a$ is the true iff $a$ is not the false, thereby confirming a conjecture made by Landini that $a \to (-a) = a$ is not provable in this subsystem. This motivates our main result, namely, soundness and completeness proofs for the first-order fragment without value-ranges with respect to a new nonclassical semantics of boolean truncation. Simply put, the widespread assumption that Grundgesetze's first-order logic is classical first-order logic is mistaken.

papers.title: Sophie Germain, math\'ematicienne extraordinaire: A story stranger than fiction. Sophie Germain, math\'{e}maticienne extraordinaire: une histoire plus \'{e}trange qu'une fiction
papers.abstract: English: Sophie Germain (1776-1831) is the first woman known for important original research in mathematics, specifically in elasticity theory and number theory. We outline Germain's recently unearthed number theory results on Fermat's Last Theorem, in the context of her life, work, and interactions with Lagrange, Legendre, and Gauss. For two centuries her accomplishment was thought to consist of a single theorem attributed to her by Legendre, the first general result towards proving Fermat's Last Theorem. But recent discoveries in her handwritten manuscripts and correspondence show that she accomplished much more, albeit forgotten. In particular, she had a plan for proving Fermat's Last Theorem in its entirety, and carried this plan far, using then new tools, e.g., congruence, modular primitive roots, and permutations. Fran\c{c}ais: Sophie Germain (1776-1831) est la premi\`ere femme connu pour des recherches originales importantes en math\'ematiques, en particulier en th\'eorie de l'\'elasticit\'e et en th\'eorie des nombres. Nous exposons les r\'esultats r\'ecemment d\'ecouverts de Germain en th\'eorie des nombres sur le dernier th\'eor\`eme de Fermat, dans le contexte de sa vie, de son oeuvre et de ses interactions avec Lagrange, Legendre et Gauss. Pendant deux si\`ecles, ses r\'esultats ont \'et\'e consid\'er\'es comme formant un seul th\'eor\`eme, attribu\'e \`a elle par Legendre, et qui \'etait le premier r\'esultat g\'en\'eral pour d\'emontrer le dernier th\'eor\`eme de Fermat. Mais des d\'ecouvertes r\'ecentes dans ses manuscrits et sa correspondance montrent qu'elle a accompli bien plus, quoique ce fut oubli\'e. En particulier, elle avait un plan pour d\'emontrer dans son int\'egralit\'e le dernier th\'eor\`eme de Fermat, et elle a men\'e loin ce plan, utilisant alors de nouveaux outils, par exemple, la congruence, les racines primitives modulaires et les permutations.
